item.title: Mahanadi IPO explained: Valuation, reserves, risks and Coal India strategy
item.description: Mahanadi Coalfields, Coal India's largest coal-producing subsidiary, is set to enter the stock market through an offer for sale of a 10% stake ...
item.dc:creator: Barkha Mathur
item.content:encoded: Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd (MCL), Coal India's largest coal-producing subsidiary, has fixed a price band of ₹129–136 per share for its upcoming initial public offering (IPO), according to a report by Reuters. The IPO will comprise an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 661,836,300 equity shares by Coal India, representing a 10 per cent stake in the Odisha-based coal producer, according to the company's red herring prospectus (RHP) dated November 13. At the upper end of the price band, MCL is valued at approximately ₹90,000 crore, Reuters reported. The issue, estimated at ₹8,981 crore, will open for public subscription on November 19 and close on November 23. Because it is a 100 per cent OFS, all of the IPO proceeds will go directly to Coal India and not into MCL's bank account. Following the sale, Coal India's shareholding in Mahanadi will come down from 100 per cent to approximately 90 per cent. The upcoming IPO marks another step in the government's plan to unlock value from its coal subsidiaries through stock-market listings.Why Mahanadi Coalfields matters to Coal IndiaIncorporated on April 3, 1992, MCL is headquartered in Sambalpur, Odisha. It operates across the Talcher and Ib Valley coalfields, two major coal-producing regions in the state. It was granted Miniratna Category-I status in December 2019. The company produced 218.31 million tonnes (MT) of coal in FY26, making it the largest single coal producer in India during the year. This accounted for approximately 21 per cent of the country's total domestic coal production and 22.4 per cent of its non-coking coal output, according to the RHP. MCL also accounted for approximately 28.4 per cent of Coal India's total production of 768.19 MT in FY26. Its contribution to the parent's non-coking coal production was even higher, at 30.8 per cent, according to the RHP. In terms of financial contribution also, Mahanadi is significant for Coal India. It reported revenue from operations of ₹30,550 crore in FY26, with profit after tax (PAT) of ₹10,698 crore. Its earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) stood at ₹16,085 crore, translating into an Ebitda margin of 47.45 per cent. Its PAT margin was 31.56 per cent. For context, Coal India's consolidated revenue from operations stood at ₹1.68 trillion in FY26, while its consolidated PAT was approximately ₹31,071 crore. Mahanadi's revenue was equivalent to roughly 18 per cent of the parent's consolidated revenue, while its profit was equivalent to about 34 per cent of the parent's consolidated PAT. According to the RHP, the Talcher and Ib Valley coalfields together had estimated geological resources (or the estimated quantity of coal present) of approximately 106.76 billion tonnes as of April 1, 2026. Mahanadi's audited coal reserves (the economically viable subset of a resource) stood at 9,840.31 million tonnes. These reserves were estimated to support around 45 years of production at FY26 levels.Why is Coal India listing its subsidiaries?1. Unlocking value from individual businesses Coal India operates through multiple subsidiaries, each with different coalfields, production profiles, resource bases, and financial performance. When these businesses remain within a single listed parent, investors primarily buy exposure to Coal India's consolidated performance. A separate listing changes this and it will give the subsidiary its own market capitalisation, share price and investor base. The listing could also help address what is known as the holding-company discount, where a parent company is valued by the market at less than the combined worth of its investments in subsidiaries. 2. Greater transparency and accountability As a listed entity, Mahanadi will have to comply with the Securities and Exchange Board of India's (Sebi's) disclosure and corporate governance requirements, including periodic financial reporting, disclosures of material developments and requirements relating to board oversight and related-party transactions. The listing also subjects the company's capital expenditure, operating costs, production targets and management decisions to greater scrutiny. 3. Monetisation and disinvestment The Mahanadi IPO is expected to generate approximately ₹8,981 crore at the upper end of the price band. The proceeds will go to Coal India, which can use the funds for its own financial and investment priorities, including capital expenditure, expansion and other strategic requirements. The government can benefit indirectly through its ownership of Coal India and the dividends it receives from the company. Coal India paid approximately ₹10,272 crore in dividends to the government in FY26, according to its chairman's statement.A larger Coal India listing strategyThe Mahanadi IPO is the third subsidiary listing in Coal India's broader programme to bring its businesses to the stock market. The sequence began with Bharat Coking Coal Ltd (BCCL), which was listed on January 19, 2026. This was followed by Central Mine Planning & Design Institute Ltd (CMPDI), which made its market debut on March 30. Another major coal-producing subsidiary, South Eastern Coalfields Ltd (SECL), has also filed its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP). Speaking at Coal India's 52nd annual general meeting, Chairman B Sairam described the subsidiary listings as an important step towards unlocking value, broadening access to capital markets and strengthening Coal India's position as a diversified listed public sector enterprise. As of November 16, CMPDI had gained more than 18 per cent since its March listing, while BCCL had declined approximately 29 per cent from its debut, Reuters reported.What risks investors should be aware aboutWhile Mahanadi's scale, profitability and resource base offer investors significant exposure to India's coal industry, the RHP also identifies several risks that could affect its business and financial performance. 1. Dependence on non-coking coal and the power sector The company listed its dependence on non-coking coal as the biggest business risk. According to the RHP, non-coking coal accounted for 97.41 per cent of its product sales in FY26. Its performance is therefore closely tied to demand from thermal power plants and other industrial consumers. Power utilities and independent power producers accounted for 68.62 per cent of sales, while the top 10 customers contributed 55.94 per cent of revenue from operations, leaving the company exposed to changes in their procurement needs and financial health. The RHP also flags delayed payments by two Andhra Pradesh power utilities. As of September 30, 2026, receivables from Andhra Pradesh Power Generation Corporation and Andhra Pradesh Power Development Company stood at about ₹1,930 crore and ₹502 crore, respectively. Such delays can strain working capital and cash flows. 2. Energy transition and long-term coal demand The longer-term transition towards renewable energy is another risk. Coal continues to dominate India's electricity generation despite the rapid expansion of renewable energy capacity. According to the Ministry of Coal, it accounts for more than 70 per cent of the country's electricity generation and close to 55 per cent of its primary energy requirements. This provides near-term demand visibility for producers such as Mahanadi. But the longer-term outlook is less certain. The Crisil report cited in Mahanadi's RHP projects India's non-coking coal demand to increase from 1,112 MT in FY25 to 1,564 MT by FY36. It also indicates that demand could decline after FY36 as renewable energy emerges as an alternative source. 3. Environmental clearances and land acquisition Coal mining requires environmental and forest clearances, mining rights and land acquisition approvals. Delays in obtaining these permissions can affect production expansion and the opening of new mines. Mahanadi specifically identifies land acquisition and resettlement and rehabilitation (R&R) bottlenecks as risks to its greenfield projects. Its operations are concentrated in Odisha's Talcher and Ib Valley coalfields. The RHP notes that the Ib Valley industrial cluster has been classified as a Severely Polluted Area under the Central Pollution Control Board's (CPCB's) pollution assessment framework. This could result in additional environmental safeguards and more stringent conditions for clearances, increasing compliance costs or delaying approvals. 4. Regulatory and taxation risks The company's operations are also exposed to changes in mining regulations, royalty rates, taxes, duties and other state-level levies. Any increase in these charges could raise the cost of production and affect margins. Changes in government policies on coal pricing, imports, allocation frameworks and environmental regulations could also alter the competitive environment. The RHP additionally records demand notices alleging production in excess of environmental clearance limits, amounting to approximately ₹2,864 crore. Mahanadi has filed a revision petition before the Coal Tribunal. 5. Production and transportation bottlenecks Coal production depends on the availability of machinery, contractors, labour and transportation infrastructure. Mahanadi identifies heavy rainfall, flooding, railway capacity constraints, delays in transportation, contractor-related disruptions and equipment breakdowns among the risks that could affect its production and dispatch operations.What comes next for India's coal industry?After the Mahanadi IPO, the proposed SECL listing will be the next important milestone for Coal India. The government is also pursuing a parallel reform programme through commercial coal mining, which allows private companies to mine and sell coal without restrictions on end-use. According to the Ministry of Coal, 141 coal mines have been auctioned commercially across 14 rounds since the launch of commercial coal mining in June 2020. These mines have a combined peak rated capacity of 366.35 MT per annum. Captive and commercial mines together produced 210.46 MT in FY26, accounting for 20.2 per cent of national coal production. For Coal India, the Mahanadi listing offers a route to monetise part of its subsidiary portfolio and establish independent valuations for its businesses. For the government, it advances the asset-monetisation agenda while retaining indirect ownership. For investors, it creates an opportunity to participate in a business with strong current earnings and substantial coal reserves.

item.title: Jimmy Tata takes on Noel, says Tata Sons listing will end culture of secrecy
item.description: Breaking his silence on the Tata group dispute, Jimmy Tata backs Chandrasekaran's third term, questions Noel Tata's veto powers and warns against restructuring Tata Sons to avoid listing ...
item.dc:creator: Nivedita Mookerji
item.content:encoded: Jimmy N Tata, the oldest trustee of Tata Trusts and younger brother of former chairman Ratan Tata, has for the first time spoken out on the dispute within the group. The 86-year-old Jimmy, who lives in a modest apartment in Pune and is often described as a recluse, has expressed concern over “unnatural, dictatorial veto powers” granted to the chairman of Tata Trusts, which is the largest shareholder in Tata Sons with a 66 per cent stake. Jimmy, who owns around a 0.81 per cent stake in Tata Sons, has backed a stock exchange listing of Tata Sons, which is at the centre of the biggest corporate battle of the time. “Listing would dismantle the pervasive culture of secrecy, impose statutory accountability, and necessitate rewriting the onerous Articles of Association (AoA) to restore the pre-1989 separation between business operations and welfare trusts,” he is understood to have said in a signed statement following a conversation with a senior trustee recently. He has termed listing a critical step. Noel Tata, chairman of Tata Trusts and nominee director on the Tata Sons board, had reiterated his opposition to listing Tata Sons at a media event on Saturday. “Listing will change the Tata way, putting profit ahead of philanthropy,” Noel, who has a 1 per cent shareholding in Tata Sons, had said. Looking at recent developments at the group, Jimmy is learnt to have stated that listing of Tata Sons, as mandated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), is “all the more critical”. Pointing out that Tata Sons previously “benefited immensely when Tata Consultancy Services was taken public under Ratan Tata”, Jimmy said that “any proposal or move by Noel Tata to break up Tata Sons into smaller entities to evade the RBI’s threshold requirements for listing is deeply damaging and contrary to public and shareholder interests, undertaken solely to preserve secrecy, avoid scrutiny, and maintain unchecked personal power.” The RBI, he said, should enforce strict timelines for listing without delay and ensure that breaking up the group is not permitted. He also sought the intervention of the government and the Charity Commissioner “to protect the original objects of the trusts for the people of India”. On the other dispute around the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran for a third term as executive chairman of Tata Sons, Jimmy has been quoted as saying: “JRD Tata valued and nurtured his key operating star performers (including Sumant Moolgaonkar, Darbari Seth, Xerxes Desai, and Rusi Modi), whereas the present leadership fails to support its proven star performer.” He said that “Noel sought to block him arbitrarily by invoking the onerous veto provisions in the amended Articles of Association without providing any justification or accountability” despite the “overwhelming support” of the Tata Sons board and “unanimous resolution” passed by Tata Trusts for Chandrasekaran’s third term. Jimmy mentioned “bumper dividend payouts” from Tata companies to shareholders, including Tata Sons, in his support for Chandrasekaran. At the Tata Sons board meeting on September 17, 2026, Noel had voted against Chandrasekaran’s third term and opposed the listing proposal. Subsequently, Noel proposed that Tata Sons could be restructured so that it could remain a privately held entity. Responding to queries linked to the current situation in Tata Trusts and other widely reported developments in the group, Jimmy said that “a central driver of this issue is the drastic alteration of the Articles of Association around 2013–2014. Historically, under the pre-1989 framework, the Articles strictly separated the welfare trusts from the commercial business operations of Tata Sons, ensuring the Trusts had no operational management role”. He added that the subsequent amendments “fundamentally overturned this balance by granting the Tata Trusts chairman unnatural, dictatorial veto powers and the right to place directors, thereby subverting the collective authority of the rest of the board”. Why is the Tata family in focus? A trustee of Sir Ratan Tata Trust (SRTT) — a key shareholder trust — since 1989, Jimmy raised the issue of family members occupying the boards of Tata Trusts. “What has transpired in recent time is that the trusts are being filled with family members of the present Tata Trusts chairman, thereby securing a degree of control over Tata Sons that was never the settlors’ intention,” he said. Jimmy argued that it is “entirely inappropriate for more than one family member to serve on a given trust; doing so effectively confers ownership rights over the trusts’ significant shareholding in Tata Sons at no consideration whatsoever”. According to Jimmy, such an arrangement is “untenable and amounts to a back-door takeover of Tata Sons”. He stressed that trustees are supposed to be custodians of public trusts that can never be dissolved, unlike private family trusts, while talking about “independent luminaries” such as Nani Palkhivala, Gautam Sarabhai, Homi Sethna, and Homi Bhabha being trustees earlier. SRTT, which was frozen by the Maharashtra Charity Commissioner earlier this year over perpetual trustee rules, allows only one-fourth of the total board strength to be perpetual or lifetime trustees under the amended law. Currently, SRTT has three perpetual trustees — Noel Tata, who is the half-brother of Ratan Tata and Jimmy Tata; Jehangir HC Jehangir, an industrialist and philanthropist; and Jimmy N Tata. The term of the fourth trustee on SRTT, Venu Srinivasan, runs until December 2026, unless renewed further. On a board of four trustees, only one can be a perpetual member. While Jimmy is not on the other key shareholder trust — Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) — he is also a trustee of some other smaller charitable trusts. What is the dispute over trustees’ tenures? Criticising the lack of uniformity in decisions, including the renewal of tenures at Tata Trusts, Jimmy said that introducing a time limit on the tenure of certain trustees while exempting others “has compromised trustee independence and concentrated authority, enabling the marginalisation or removal of trustees who dissent”. Citing the example of Venu Srinivasan, Jimmy said he was targeted because he “opposed induction of Noel’s son into SRTT”. Neville Tata, Noel Tata’s son, is a trustee of SDTT but not of SRTT. Neville and his sisters, Leah and Maya, are on some other trusts’ boards as well. Jimmy, who mostly stays away from public outings, including Tata Trusts meetings, was at the funeral of his elder brother Ratan Tata on October 10, 2024, in Mumbai.

item.content:encoded: Sensex Today | Stock Market LIVE Updates, Monday, Nov 16, 2026: The Nifty50 and the Sensex rose as oil prices continued to decline on improved supply outlook.  As of 1:00 PM, the Sensex rose 446.63 points or 0.55 per cent to 82,039.08, and the Nifty50 was up 115.40 points or 0.46 per cent to 25,259.70. Eicher Motors, Asian Paints, and Bharti Airtel were the top gainers in the Nifty50 index.  In the broader market, the Nifty MidCap 100 and the Nifty SmallCap 100 fell 0.41 per cent and 0.78 per cent, respectively.  Sector-wise, the Nifty FMCG rose the most, while the Nifty Realty and the Nifty Metal declined the most.

item.title: Alibaba says Qwen4-Max cuts task costs by 60%, boosts cyber safeguards
item.description: Alibaba's Qwen4-Max AI model claims to cut average task costs by 60% while using fewer tokens and strengthening safeguards against cybersecurity threats and other risks ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Alibaba says Qwen4-Max cuts task costs by 60%, boosts cyber safeguards

Alibaba says Qwen4-Max cuts task costs by 60%, boosts cyber safeguards Alibaba's Qwen4-Max AI model claims to cut average task costs by 60% while using fewer tokens and strengthening safeguards against cybersecurity threats and other risks

Alibaba's Qwen4-Max is built on an upgraded sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which allows it to activate only a portion of its total parameters for each token processed. (Image: Bloomberg)

Akshita Singh New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 12:04 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Alibaba on Monday launched Qwen4-Max, its latest flagship artificial intelligence (AI) model, claiming it reduces average task costs by around 60 per cent while strengthening safeguards against cybersecurity threats and other risks.    The company said the model outperforms its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, on complex professional tasks while using 35 per cent fewer tokens in high-effort reasoning mode.   According to the company's press release, Qwen4-Max has 2.4 trillion parameters, native vision capabilities and a context window of one million tokens.    Alibaba described it as the "most capable model in the Qwen family to date".   Model architecture and benchmark performance   Qwen4-Max is built on an upgraded sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which allows it to activate only a portion of its total parameters for each token processed, the company said.

Although the model has 2.4 trillion total parameters, it activates 71 billion parameters per token, 25% fewer than Qwen3.8-Max at the same overall scale, according to Alibaba.   The company said Qwen4-Max outperformed Qwen3.8-Max on its proprietary Work360 benchmark, which evaluates performance across 721 specialised fields.   In high-effort reasoning mode, the model used 35% fewer tokens and reduced the average cost per task by around 60 per cent.    Qwen4-Max also ranked sixth on Code Arena, a real-world coding leaderboard.    Alibaba reported strong results on other benchmarks covering agent workflows, workplace productivity and visual reasoning, including Agents' Last Exam, Vals Index, JobBench and Chartography.   Applications in professional workflows   The model is designed to handle tasks across 3D modelling, game development, precision manufacturing, finance, law and healthcare.

Alibaba said Qwen4-Max also supports cloud resource scheduling. In benchmark testing, its scheduling capabilities reduced data-annotation model call costs by an average of 9% and increased offline CPU rescheduling speeds by more than 14 times.   In automotive manufacturing, the model can assist with production-line planning, part design and machining verification. During a company demonstration, it reduced manual workpiece programming time by 95 per cent, from around 475 minutes to 24 minutes, by identifying excessive cutting and insufficient material removal before machining began.   Scientific research applications   Alibaba also reported using Qwen4-Max for an experiment involving Alzheimer's research. The model handled tasks covering target research, molecular design and computational evaluation.

During the workflow, it autonomously executed 454 tool calls and 3,239 metric evaluations to design and optimise 24 candidate molecules, according to the company.   Cybersecurity and safety measures   Alibaba said it incorporated security checks into software engineering training alongside functionality tests to address vulnerabilities such as code injection, memory-safety flaws and broken access controls.   The company also filtered training data according to task intent. It retained defensive cybersecurity material used for vulnerability detection and remediation while removing content related to offensive cyberattacks.   In addition, Alibaba introduced dedicated safety datasets and post-training improvements to strengthen protections against chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) risks.   According to Reuters, Alibaba said its internal testing had found no evidence of significant high-risk capabilities in the model. The company also said it had strengthened safeguards against potential misuse in areas such as cybercrime and hazardous materials.

Availability and pricing   Qwen4-Max is available through Alibaba's QwenCloud platform via its Token Plan and application programming interface (API). Users can also access it through QwenWork and QwenStudio.   Alibaba has priced input tokens with an implicit cache hit at $0.075 per million tokens. The company said smaller, open-weight models from the Qwen4 series would be released to developers worldwide.
